name: AI Layer Model
author: Logan Smith
scope: An OSI-inspired reference model of runtime responsibilities, not a literal OSI mapping or fixed execution pipeline.

layers.name: Hardware / compute
layers.responsibility: Provide the physical capacity to execute work.
layers.question: What hardware runs it?
layers.boundary: Processors, accelerators, memory, storage and the physical execution environment.

layers.name: Runtime / inference engine
layers.responsibility: Load, schedule, execute and serve a model.
layers.question: What loads and runs the model?
layers.boundary: Model loading, execution kernels, batching, scheduling and serving. A managed service still has these responsibilities.

layers.name: Model
layers.question: Which model is doing the work?
layers.boundary: The model architecture, weights and released artifact. A model call is an operation using the model, not the definition of this layer.

layers.name: Inference strategy / reasoning
layers.responsibility: Shape how a model call is run.
layers.question: How are we using the model for this call?
layers.boundary: Supported decoding settings, prompting strategies and reasoning or output budgets. Capabilities depend on the selected model; reasoning capability can also be a property of L3.

layers.name: Context / memory
layers.responsibility: Supply the information available to a model call.
layers.question: What information can it see?
layers.boundary: Instructions, conversation, retrieved content, returned tool results and relevant stored state. Persistent memory is optional.

layers.name: Tools / capabilities
layers.responsibility: Expose capabilities a model-driven system can request.
layers.question: What can it request or do beyond generating text?
layers.boundary: Functions, APIs, retrieval, file operations and other capabilities. The tool is the capability; its returned information may become L5 context. Enforcement remains with the application and tool.

layers.name: Agentic control loop
layers.responsibility: Decide the next action, continuation and stop condition.
layers.question: What decides the next step or when to stop?
layers.boundary: Goal-directed control, observation, decisions and termination. This is one responsibility in an agent, not the entire assembled agent or its user interface.

layers.name: Orchestration
layers.responsibility: Coordinate distinct parts, models, agents or workstreams.
layers.question: What coordinates the work?
layers.boundary: Routing, delegation, workflow coordination, handoffs and shared-state coordination. Multiple agents are optional; distinguish coordination from a single control loop.

layers.name: Interface / delivery
layers.responsibility: Deliver the system and its results to people or other systems.
layers.question: How is the result used or delivered?
layers.boundary: Chat, application surfaces, client rendering, integrations and delivered endpoints. An endpoint may also expose L2 serving; inspect its actual responsibility.

principles: Place responsibilities rather than marketing labels.
Products, protocols and patterns can span layers.
Separate responsibilities owned by an item from dependencies and configured integrations.
Model calls and tasks can revisit components; numbers do not define execution order.
A typical tool-using agent composes multiple responsibilities; memory, tools and multi-agent coordination are not universally required.
Build and training work is a companion view; released model artifacts hand off to runtime L3.
A layer mapping identifies questions and control points; it is not a security certification.
